L67@P1: Historical Note
L68@P1: Nolan Bushnell grew up in a small town near Salt Lake City, Utah. As a teenager, he repaired
L69@P1: television sets while also working at his father’s cement contracting business. Bushnell received
L70@P1: his first exposure to computer games attending the University of Utah as a computer graphics
L71@P1: student. While there, he, like other computer engineer students, played math and simple video
L72@P1: games on large and expensive mainframe computers. Bushnell also worked a part-time job at an
L73@P1: amusement park arcade, where he became familiar with coin-op electro-mechanical games. After
L74@P1: college, Bushnell combined his knowledge of computers, televisions, and coin-op games to make
L75@P1: the first commercial video game, Computer Space. Based on an MIT space game, Spacewar!,
L76@P1: Bushnell licensed the game to Nutting Associates. However Computer Space failed to generate
L77@P1: much excitement or fanfare. Believing that he could do better on his own, Bushnell, along with
L78@P1: his business partner Ted Dabney, founded Syzygy; when they were informed that the name was
L79@P1: taken, they changed it to Atari, Inc. Once Atari was officially founded in 1972, Bushnell and
L80@P1: Dabney hired engineer Al Alcorn to design a table-like ping pong game. The result was Pong—
L81@P1: the simple tennis-like game that featured two parallel bars and a moving dot—which ultimately
L82@P1: transformed the video game industry.
L83@P1: Following Pong, Atari continued to experience tremendous success. Along with Pong sequels
L84@P1-2: (Doubles Pong, Super Pong, Quadrapong, and other variations), there were other subsequent hits Brian Sutton-Smith Library and Archives of Play Cort and Barbara Allen Atari Packaging Design Collection Finding Aid
L85@P2: August 2016 Page 3
L86@P2: including: Gran Trak 10, Tank, Crash ‘N Score, Breakout (a game that was famously designed
L87@P2: by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak—though their design, too complicated for mass production,
L88@P2: was not used in the final product), Night Driver, Subs, Le Mans, and Fire Truck. In 1975, Atari
L89@P2: created a home version of Pong (appropriately called Home Pong), which was marketed
L90@P2: exclusively at Sears and quickly sold 150,000 units under the Sears Tele-Games label. Two years
L91@P2: later, Atari released another consumer product, the Video Computer System (later rebranded the
L92@P2: Atari 2600), a game system that used video game cartridges.
L93@P2: The Atari home consoles revolutionized the experience of gaming forever, bringing the exciting
L94@P2: fun of the arcade into the homes of millions. Asteroids, Berzerk, Breakout, Pole Position,
L95@P2: Robotron 2084, and Surround soon became games that many Americans could now play within
L96@P2: their own homes. The 2600 became a substitute for many arcade games in the late 1970s and
L97@P2: early 1980s, in turn maiming the coin-op industry. In 1982, Atari released the higher-end Atari
L98@P2: 5200 SuperSystem, a more powerful home gaming machine with superior graphics capabilities;
L99@P2: however, it only sold one million units. Following the release of the 5200, the Atari 7800
L100@P2: ProSystem hit store shelves in 1986, followed in turn by several other consoles before Atari
L101@P2: released its final system, the Atari Jaguar, in 1993.
L102@P2: Collection Scope and Content Note
L103@P2: The Cort and Barbara Allen Atari packaging design collection comprises 41 linear feet of
L104@P2: materials with dates ranging from 1976 to 1984. Materials include drawings, photographs,
L105@P2: proofs, preliminary package mockups, drafts of manual scripts, unused packaging, box flats,
L106@P2: designs, and other internal documents used in the design and production of Atari’s packaging
L107@P2: and manuals for home console video games, computer games, game consoles, and handheld
L108@P2: games. There are materials related to the Atari 400, Atari 800, Atari 2600, Atari 5200
L109@P2: SuperSystem, various home Pong consoles, and the Atari Touch Me, as well as materials related
L110@P2: to several unreleased devices. Additional scope and content notes can be found within the
L111@P2: Contents List section of this finding aid. (Oversized materials may require advance notice to
L112@P2: retrieve for researchers.)
L113@P2: The Cort and Barbara Allen Atari packaging design collection has been arranged into four series,
L114@P2: two of which have been further divided into subseries. The materials are housed in 16 archival
L115@P2-3: document boxes and 5 flat file drawers. Brian Sutton-Smith Library and Archives of Play Cort and Barbara Allen Atari Packaging Design Collection Finding Aid
L116@P3: August 2016 Page 4
L117@P3: Related Materials
L118@P3: The Strong is also home to the Atari Coin-Op Division corporate records, which comprise 600
L119@P3: linear feet of game design documents, memos, focus group reports, market research reports,
L120@P3: marketing materials, arcade cabinet drawings, schematics, artwork, photographs, videos, and
L121@P3: publication material. The Strong acquired several unique museum objects with this accession lot
L122@P3: of archival materials; as a result, ICHEG’s collections include two computer towers which
L123@P3: operated at Atari, Inc. (a mobile unit and a stationary tower) and a binder which notable game
L124@P3: designer Ed Logg utilized in the creation of iconic Atari game Asteroids. For additional
L125@P3: information on the coin-op division of Atari, see also the Atari design concept sketches, 1973-
L126@P3: 1991, in the Brian Sutton-Smith Library and Archives of Play. These design sketches provide a
L127@P3: further look into Atari’s arcade cabinet designs.
L128@P3: Also acquired alongside the Atari Coin-Op Division corporate records were the remaining
L129@P3: corporate records of Tengen, Inc., a wholly-owned subsidiary of Atari Games which operated
L130@P3: between 1987 and 1994 (see also the Tengen, Inc. records, 1985-1995, in the Brian Sutton-Smith
L131@P3: Library and Archives of Play).
L132@P3: The Strong is also home to a large collection of Atari coin-operated arcade games, ranging from
L133@P3: best-sellers such as Pong, Asteroids, and Centipede, to lesser known prototypes such as Maze
L134@P3: Invaders. In addition, The Strong also houses several Atari home consoles and many Atari home
L135@P3: console games. They can be viewed via the Online Collections section of The Strong’s website.

L151@P4: Series I: Insert designs, 1976-1984
L152@P4: Scope and Content Note: This series contains the manual design materials for
L153@P4: many of Atari’s home console games and hardware, as well as designs for various
L154@P4: inserts within Atari products. This series has been subdivided into subseries,
L155@P4: focusing on English game manual designs, French game manual designs, PAL
L156@P4: region manual designs, hardware manual designs, and miscellaneous insert
L157@P4: designs. The Atari insert design materials range from preliminary layouts and
L158@P4: sketches to final proofs and printed material.
L159@P4: Subseries A: English game manual designs

L161@P4: game manuals for the Atari Video Computer System (later rebranded as the Atari

L163@P4: Atari Home Computer Division, which encompassed all 8-bit Atari home
L164@P4: computers (such as the Atari 400 and Atari 800). The manual designs range from
L165@P4: preliminary layouts and sketches to final proofs and printed manuals.

L307@P8: The Phase Alternating Line (PAL) region is a television publication territory that
L308@P8: covers most of Asia, Africa, Europe, South America and Oceania, in contrast to
L309@P8: the NTSC standard used in Japan and nearly all of North America. Therefore, the
L310@P8: PAL game manuals consist of English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish
L311@P8: versions of the instructions. The manual designs are mostly proofs and final
L312@P8: proofs.
